title: Login handler does not regenerate the session id after authentication (session fixation)
evidence: I read the entire login chain: app/routes/index.js:34 registers app.post("/login", sessionHandler.handleLoginRequest) with no middleware in front of it, and handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-118) verifies the password via userDAO.validateLogin and then, on success, writes req.session.userId directly at line 116 with no call to req.session.regenerate() beforehand -- the comment block at lines 104-115 describes exactly this fix and it is not applied. This is the asymmetric case: the signup handler a few lines later (app/routes/session.js:234, this.handleSignup) does call req.session.regenerate() before setting userId, so the codebase demonstrates the fix exists but was left out of the login path specifically. The session is created with saveUninitialized:true (server.js:84) before login, so a pre-login session id already exists and is reused as-is after authentication.
impact: An attacker who fixes a victim's pre-login session id (by setting the cookie over the app's plaintext HTTP connection, or via a subdomain) inherits the victim's authenticated session once the victim logs in, without ever knowing the victim's password.
fix: Call req.session.regenerate() and re-set req.session.userId inside the callback immediately after userDAO.validateLogin succeeds, mirroring what handleSignup already does at line 234.

title: POST /benefits lets any logged-in user modify any other user's benefit record with no admin check
evidence: The middleware chain in front of this route is only isLoggedIn (app/routes/index.js:24,56); isAdmin (sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware, defined at app/routes/session.js:25-34 and aliased at index.js:27) is never applied to it -- the correct chain is written out but commented at index.js:57-60 ('Fix for A7 - checks user role to implement Function Level Access Control ... app.post("/benefits", isLoggedIn, isAdmin, benefitsHandler.updateBenefits)'). The handler itself (app/routes/benefits.js:29-54) reads userId straight from req.body and passes it to benefitsDAO.updateBenefits(userId, benefitStartDate, ...) (app/data/benefits-dao.js:23-40), which runs usersCol.update({_id: parseInt(userId)}, {$set:{benefitStartDate}}) with no ownership or role check anywhere on the path.
impact: Any authenticated non-admin user can POST an arbitrary userId and benefitStartDate to change any other user's benefit start date, and can probe/enumerate valid numeric user ids (assigned sequentially by getNextSequence) to do so at scale -- a function meant to be admin-only is reachable by every logged-in account.
fix: Add the isAdmin middleware to both the GET and POST /benefits routes as the commented-out code at index.js:57-60 already shows, and additionally verify server-side that the target userId is a legitimate operation for the caller's role.

title: GET /allocations/:userId loads any user's allocation data by id with no ownership check
evidence: The only middleware in front of this route is isLoggedIn (index.js:24, 63); there is no comparison anywhere to req.session.userId. The handler (app/routes/allocations.js:11-31) takes userId straight from req.params (line 16-18, commented-out fix right above it at lines 12-15 says to take it from req.session instead) and passes it unchecked to allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold, which queries by that id and renders the result back to the caller.
impact: Any authenticated user can view any other user's stock/funds/bonds allocation data by changing the :userId path segment to another user's numeric id (ids are sequential, assigned by getNextSequence in app/data/user-dao.js), a classic horizontal privilege escalation / IDOR.
fix: Ignore the userId route parameter for authorization purposes and use req.session.userId (the fix already sketched in the comment at allocations.js:12-15) to decide whose allocations to load, or verify req.params.userId === req.session.userId before querying.

title: Signup stores the user's password in plaintext with no hashing
evidence: this.addUser (app/data/user-dao.js:17-47) builds the user document with the raw password value taken verbatim from the signup form (app/routes/session.js:189-198, req.body.password passed straight into userDAO.addUser at line 220) and inserts it as-is; the bcrypt-hashed alternative (bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())) is present only as a comment at lines 26-30 and is never called -- the bcrypt-nodejs module is required at line 1 but unused anywhere in the file.
impact: Any read access to the users collection (a backup, a misconfigured export, or any other injection/IDOR finding that can dump the collection) discloses every user's password in cleartext, enabling immediate account takeover here and on any other service where the password is reused.
fix: Hash the password with bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync()) before storing it, as shown in the commented-out fix at lines 26-30, and migrate existing plaintext passwords on next login.

title: Login failure branches render different messages for an unknown user versus a wrong password
evidence: I read every failure branch of handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-119). userDAO.validateLogin (app/data/user-dao.js:57-94) sets err.noSuchUser when no document matches the username and err.invalidPassword when the password comparison fails. The login handler branches on that: err.noSuchUser renders loginError: invalidUserNameErrorMessage ('Invalid username', line 85) while err.invalidPassword renders loginError: invalidPasswordErrorMessage ('Invalid password', line 94) -- a shared, account-agnostic errorMessage is defined at line 59 and explicitly commented out at lines 86 and 96 ('Fix for A2-2 Broken Auth - Uses identical error for both username, password error').
impact: An attacker can enumerate valid usernames by submitting a guessed username with any password and reading which of the two messages comes back, narrowing a credential-stuffing or brute-force attack to accounts that are known to exist.
fix: Return the same generic message (the errorMessage constant already defined at line 59) for both the noSuchUser and invalidPassword branches, and take the same amount of time on both paths.

title: Signup password validator accepts a single-character password
evidence: validateSignup (app/routes/session.js:138-187) is the only gate before userDAO.addUser stores the password; its PASS_RE at line 144 matches any 1-to-20-character string with no character-class requirement, so a password of "a" passes PASS_RE.test(password) at line 171 and is accepted. The user-visible error text at lines 172-173 claims '8 to 18 characters including numbers, lowercase and uppercase letters', but the regex enforcing it does not check any of that; the actually strong rule is written out and commented at lines 146-149 (/^(?=.*\d)(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z]).{8,}$/) and is never used.
impact: Accounts can be created with trivially guessable one-character passwords, making credential stuffing and brute force against those accounts immediate.
fix: Replace PASS_RE with the stronger rule already present in the comment at lines 146-149, or an equivalent length-and-complexity check, and enforce it server-side.

title: State-changing profile update (bank account, routing, SSN) has no CSRF protection
evidence: I read the full middleware chain from server.js top to bottom: the csurf package is required only in a comment (server.js:7, 'const csrf = require(\'csurf\');'), and the entire block that would mount it and expose res.locals.csrftoken (server.js:104-113) is commented out; app.use(csrf()) never runs anywhere in server.js, and no other file in app/routes requires or checks a csrf token. The route chain in front of POST /profile is only isLoggedIn (index.js:24, 48); the handler (app/routes/profile.js:40-107) changes bankAcc, bankRouting, ssn, dob and address for req.session.userId with only a session cookie required to authenticate the request -- no token or Origin/Referer check anywhere in the chain.
impact: A malicious page the logged-in victim visits can auto-submit a cross-site POST to /profile and silently change the victim's bank account and routing numbers or SSN on file, since the browser attaches the session cookie automatically and the app never checks for a token.
fix: Uncomment and mount the csurf middleware before the routes are registered (app.use(csrf()) in server.js, before routes(app, db) is called), render the token into every form, and validate it on every state-changing route including /profile, /contributions, /benefits and /memos.

title: Login endpoint has no attempt limit, lockout or delay
evidence: This route has no middleware at all in front of the handler -- not even isLoggedIn -- so nothing stands between an anonymous caller and userDAO.validateLogin. I checked package.json for a limiter dependency (grepped for 'limit'/'rate') and found none, checked server.js's whole middleware stack (favicon, bodyParser, session, static) for any request-counting middleware, and read handleLoginRequest (app/routes/session.js:53-119) end to end: it calls userDAO.validateLogin on every request with no counter, no lockout flag on the user document, and no delay before responding.
impact: An attacker can submit unlimited password guesses per username (or, combined with the enumeration finding above, per confirmed-valid username) with no throttling, making online brute force and credential-stuffing against this endpoint practical.
fix: Add a per-account and per-IP rate limiter (e.g. express-rate-limit or a lockout counter stored with the user document) in front of app.post("/login", ...) and reject further attempts after a small number of failures within a time window.

title: Session cookie is issued with no Secure flag and no absolute expiry
evidence: I read the whole express-session configuration block (server.js:78-102): it sets secret, saveUninitialized:true and resave:true but never sets a cookie object, so there is no secure, no maxAge, and no sameSite -- the fix comments right below it (lines 87-100) show the intended cookie:{httpOnly:true} plus a note that 'maxAge' and HTTPS are both still needed and are not enabled. The server itself only ever listens over plain HTTP (server.js:144-147, 'Insecure HTTP connection'), so even the default cookie is transmitted unencrypted, and with no maxAge the underlying express session in Mongo/memory has no absolute lifetime -- only client-side session-cookie deletion on browser close bounds it, and req.session.destroy() at logout (session.js:122) is the only expiry path.
impact: The session cookie can be captured by network interception (no Secure flag over the app's plain-HTTP deployment) and, once issued, has no server-enforced absolute timeout, so a captured or fixed session id remains valid indefinitely until the user explicitly logs out.
fix: Set cookie:{ secure: true, httpOnly: true, sameSite: 'strict', maxAge: <a bounded value> } in the session() call once the app is served over HTTPS, and enforce an absolute session lifetime server-side independent of activity.

title: Application server only accepts plaintext HTTP, exposing every credential and session cookie in transit
evidence: server.js requires the `http` module (line 12) and starts the whole Express app with `http.createServer(app).listen(...)` at line 145, right after a commented-out `https.createServer(httpsOptions, app)` block (lines 149-155) that reads the TLS key/cert from artifacts/cert/. The comment directly above, `// Insecure HTTP connection` (line 144), confirms no TLS path exists at runtime. Every request this server ever answers -- including the login POST at /login with the userName/password body handled in app/routes/session.js, and the session cookie set by the `session()` middleware at line 78 -- travels as cleartext.
impact: Anyone able to observe network traffic between the client and this server (a shared network, a compromised router, a man-in-the-middle) can read login credentials, session cookies, and every field submitted on the profile page (SSN, date of birth, bank account and routing numbers) as they cross the wire.
fix: Terminate TLS at the application or a reverse proxy: uncomment the https.createServer block (or equivalent), serve HTTP only to redirect to HTTPS, and set the session cookie's `secure` flag once TLS is in place.

title: User passwords are stored and compared in plaintext instead of being hashed
evidence: In `UserDAO.addUser`, the `password` field taken directly from the signup request body (app/routes/session.js `handleSignup` -> `userDAO.addUser(userName, firstName, lastName, password, email, ...)`) is placed into the `user` document verbatim at line 25; the bcrypt-hashed alternative at line 29 (`password: bcrypt.hashSync(password, bcrypt.genSaltSync())`) is commented out, so it never runs, even though the `bcrypt-nodejs` module is required at the top of the file. This plaintext document is inserted into MongoDB at line 45 (`usersCol.insert(user, ...)`). Consistently, `validateLogin`'s `comparePassword` helper at line 61 does a raw `fromDB === fromUser` string comparison against that stored value; the `bcrypt.compareSync` call that would only work against a hash is commented out at line 65.
impact: Anyone who reads the `users` collection -- via a database compromise, a backup, an admin with DB access, or any of the NoSQL-injection paths elsewhere in this codebase -- recovers every user's actual login password, not a hash. Because users commonly reuse passwords, this also compromises their accounts on other services.
fix: Hash passwords with bcrypt (or argon2id) before storage, as the commented-out code at line 29 already shows how to do, and compare with `bcrypt.compareSync` at line 65 instead of `===`; use a work factor of at least 12 for bcrypt.

title: SSN and date of birth are written to the database in plaintext; encryption code exists but is disabled
evidence: `ProfileDAO.updateUser` receives `ssn`, `dob`, `bankAcc` and `bankRouting` straight from the profile form (app/routes/profile.js `handleProfileUpdate` reads them from `req.body` and passes them through unmodified) and assigns them onto the `user` object at lines 61-66 (ssn, dob) and 55-59 (bankAcc, bankRouting) with no transformation. `users.update(..., { $set: user }, ...)` at line 78 writes that object straight to MongoDB. The file even contains a working AES/PBKDF2 encrypt-then-store routine (`createIV`, `encrypt`, `decrypt`, lines 15-40) and the call sites that would use it (`user.ssn = encrypt(ssn)` etc., lines 67-76), but the entire block is commented out, so none of it runs.
impact: Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and bank account/routing numbers for every user sit in the database as plaintext. A database compromise, an unencrypted backup, or an operator with read access to the `users` collection obtains SSNs and full bank details directly, enabling identity theft and financial fraud.
fix: Re-enable the existing encrypt/decrypt helpers (or use a maintained field-level encryption library) so ssn, dob, bankAcc and bankRouting are encrypted before the `$set` write, and decrypted only when displayed to the record's owner.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: The session-signing secret and the AES encryption key are printed to the console on every application start
evidence: `config` is built at line 10 by merging config/env/all.js (which sets `cookieSecret: "session_cookie_secret_key_here"` at all.js:8 and `cryptoKey: "a_secure_key_for_crypto_here"` at all.js:9) with the active environment file. `util.inspect(config, false, null)` at line 13 dumps that whole merged object -- secrets included -- to stdout every time the process starts, which happens on every deploy and every dev restart.
impact: Anyone with access to the application's stdout/stderr -- a log aggregator, a CI job log, a container platform's log viewer, or a co-tenant on a shared logging pipeline -- obtains the express-session signing secret (enough to forge any user's session cookie) and the AES key intended to protect SSN/DOB fields.
fix: Never log a config object that carries secrets; log an allowlist of non-sensitive keys, or redact `cookieSecret`/`cryptoKey` before logging, and load both from environment variables rather than the committed source.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Database seed script logs full user records, including plaintext passwords, to the console
evidence: `USERS_TO_INSERT` (lines 12-37) contains full user objects whose `password` field is a plaintext value (`"Admin_123"`, `"User1_123"`, `"User2_123"` at lines 18, 27, 35). Before inserting them, line 99 serializes and logs every one of these objects verbatim with `console.log(JSON.stringify(user))`, printing each plaintext password to stdout.
impact: Whoever can read the output of this reset script -- CI logs, an operator's terminal history, a log-shipping pipeline -- obtains the plaintext seed credentials, including the admin account's password.
fix: Log only non-sensitive identifiers (e.g. userName) when reporting seeded users, never the full record, and combine with hashing the password before insertion (see the user-dao.js finding).

title: Admin benefits page loads full user documents -- including plaintext passwords, SSN and bank details -- with no field projection
evidence: `getAllNonAdminUsers` runs `usersCol.find({...}).toArray(...)` with no projection, so every field of every non-admin user document -- password (stored in plaintext, see data-password-plaintext-storage), ssn, dob, bankAcc, bankRouting -- is returned. app/routes/benefits.js `displayBenefits` (line 19-25) passes this array straight into `res.render("benefits", { users, ... })`. The current benefits.html template (lines 47-66) only prints `firstName`, `lastName` and `benefitStartDate`, so the current HTTP response body does not include the other fields, but the full sensitive record for every employee reaches the template rendering context on this page, reachable by any authenticated user whose session satisfies `isAdminUserMiddleware`.
impact: Every field of every non-admin user's record, including their cleartext password and financial PII, is loaded into memory and handed to the view layer on a page rendered for admin users; a future template change, a templating bug, or a debug/error path that dumps locals would disclose it directly to the admin's browser.
fix: Project only the fields the benefits view needs, e.g. `usersCol.find({...}, { projection: { firstName: 1, lastName: 1, benefitStartDate: 1 } })`, so sensitive fields never leave the database layer for this use case.

title: NoSQL injection via MongoDB $where built from the allocations threshold query parameter
evidence: app/routes/allocations.js reads `const { threshold } = req.query;` at line 20 and passes it unmodified to `allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold(userId, threshold, ...)` at line 23. In app/data/allocations-dao.js, `getByUserIdAndThreshold`'s inner `searchCriteria` builds a MongoDB `$where` clause by interpolating the raw `threshold` string into a JavaScript expression string (line 78), which is then passed to `allocationsCol.find(searchCriteria())` at line 86 with no sanitization or type coercion (only `userId` is parsed with `parseInt`, `threshold` is not). `$where` executes its string as JavaScript on the MongoDB server for every document.
impact: An authenticated user can supply a `threshold` value such as `1'; return true; var x='` to close the quoted string early and inject arbitrary JavaScript into the server-side `$where` evaluation, letting them read every user's allocation records regardless of the intended per-user filter, or supply an infinite loop to exhaust server resources (denial of service against the shared MongoDB process).
fix: Do not use `$where` for a numeric comparison at all: validate `threshold` is an integer (e.g. `parseInt(threshold, 10)` with an explicit range check as the commented-out fix in the file already shows) and use a plain query object such as `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }` instead of a `$where` string.

title: Server-side code execution via eval() on the contributions preTax field
evidence: app/routes/index.js line 52 wires `app.post("/contributions", isLoggedIn, contributionsHandler.handleContributionsUpdate)`. `handleContributionsUpdate` in app/routes/contributions.js passes `req.body.preTax` directly into `eval()` at line 32 with no validation beforehand; the only validation (isNaN, negative, sum > 30) runs afterward on the already-evaluated result.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit a POST to /contributions with `preTax` set to arbitrary JavaScript, e.g. `require('child_process').execSync('...')`, achieving full remote code execution in the Node.js server process.
fix: Replace eval() with a safe numeric parse such as `parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10)` (the file's own commented-out fix) or `Number()`, never evaluating request data as code.

title: Server-side code execution via eval() on the contributions afterTax field
evidence: Same handler and route wiring as the preTax finding: `handleContributionsUpdate` (reached via POST /contributions, guarded only by isLoggedIn) passes `req.body.afterTax` directly into `eval()` at line 33 with no prior validation.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit a POST to /contributions with `afterTax` set to arbitrary JavaScript, achieving full remote code execution in the Node.js server process.
fix: Replace eval() with `parseInt(req.body.afterTax, 10)` or `Number()`, never evaluating request data as code.

title: Server-side code execution via eval() on the contributions roth field
evidence: Same handler and route wiring as the preTax finding: `handleContributionsUpdate` (reached via POST /contributions, guarded only by isLoggedIn) passes `req.body.roth` directly into `eval()` at line 34 with no prior validation.
impact: Any authenticated user can submit a POST to /contributions with `roth` set to arbitrary JavaScript, achieving full remote code execution in the Node.js server process.
fix: Replace eval() with `parseInt(req.body.roth, 10)` or `Number()`, never evaluating request data as code.

title: Open redirect on /learn via unvalidated query-string URL
evidence: The GET /learn route handler at app/routes/index.js lines 70-73 takes `req.query.url` straight from the query string and passes it to `res.redirect()` with no allowlist, no relative-path check, and no scheme check; the comment on the preceding line even labels this "Insecure way to handle redirects".
impact: An attacker can craft a link such as `https://victim-app/learn?url=https://evil.example/phish` that the victim's browser trusts as originating from the legitimate site, enabling phishing or OAuth-token theft via open redirect.
fix: Validate the destination against an allowlist of known-safe relative paths or hosts before calling res.redirect(), and reject absolute URLs to third-party hosts.

title: SSRF in the research page via unvalidated url query parameter fetched server-side
snippet:
const url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol;
            return needle.get(url, (error, newResponse, body) => {
evidence: GET /research is wired with only the isLoggedIn middleware (app/routes/index.js line 76). `displayResearch` builds `url` by concatenating `req.query.url` and `req.query.symbol` directly (line 15) and hands it to `needle.get(url, ...)` (line 16) with no host allowlist, scheme check, or private-IP block; the response body is then written straight back to the client at lines 22-27.
impact: Any authenticated user can make the server issue arbitrary HTTP requests to internal-only hosts or cloud metadata services (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`) and have the full response reflected back to them, enabling internal network reconnaissance, credential theft from metadata endpoints, and bypass of network-level access controls.
fix: Validate the destination against an allowlist of permitted hosts/schemes, resolve and re-check the IP against private/link-local ranges before connecting, and never reflect the raw response of an arbitrary server-side request back to the client.

title: Catastrophic-backtracking regular expression validates the profile bankRouting field
evidence: `handleProfileUpdate` (POST /profile, guarded only by isLoggedIn) destructures `bankRouting` straight from `req.body` at line 49 and runs it through `regexPattern.test(bankRouting)` at line 61, where `regexPattern` is `/([0-9]+)+\#/` — a nested quantifier `(X+)+` with no length cap on the input, applied before any length validation.
impact: A logged-in user can submit a bankRouting value of a few dozen digits with no trailing `#` (e.g. `"1111111111111111111111111111111!"`) to trigger catastrophic backtracking in this regex, pinning the single-threaded Node.js event loop at 100% CPU for a long time and denying service to every user of the shared server.
fix: Remove the redundant outer quantifier — use `/[0-9]+\#/` (the fix already noted in this file's own comment) — and cap the input length before testing it against any regex.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Unauthenticated login username written to the log without neutralizing control characters
snippet: console.log("Error: attempt to login with invalid user: ", userName);
evidence: `handleLoginRequest` (POST /login, no authentication required) destructures `userName` from `req.body` at line 55 and, when `userDAO.validateLogin` reports no such user, writes it unmodified into `console.log` at line 64. The surrounding comment (lines 66-80) explicitly documents this as a known log-injection gap and shows the CRLF-stripping fix that was left commented out.
impact: An unauthenticated attacker can submit a userName containing CR/LF sequences to forge additional, fake log lines (for example a bogus successful-login entry), misleading anyone auditing the application's logs; if these logs are later rendered in a browser-based log viewer without escaping, this becomes stored XSS in that viewer.
fix: Strip or encode CR/LF and other control characters from userName before logging (e.g. `userName.replace(/[\r\n]/g, '_')`), or use a structured logger that keeps the message template fixed and carries the value as a separate, escaped field.

title: Stored XSS: memo body is rendered through marked() with template auto-escaping disabled
evidence: POST /memos (guarded only by isLoggedIn) passes `req.body.memo` unmodified to `memosDAO.insert` (app/routes/memos.js line 13), which stores it verbatim (app/data/memos-dao.js lines 15-24). `displayMemos` then renders every stored memo through `{{ marked(doc.memo) }}` at app/views/memos.html line 31. server.js line 137 sets `swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false })` for the whole application, so swig performs no HTML-escaping on this output, and marked() (v0.3.5, per package.json) converts the memo's markdown to raw HTML that is emitted into the page as-is.
impact: Any authenticated user can post a memo containing HTML/JS payloads (e.g. an `` or a markdown link using a `javascript:` URI) that executes in the browser of every other authenticated user who views the shared /memos page, letting the attacker hijack any viewer's session.
fix: Re-enable swig's autoescape (remove `autoescape: false` in server.js), and additionally run the markdown-to-HTML output of marked() through an HTML sanitizer such as DOMPurify immediately before rendering, since marked's own deprecated `sanitize` option is not a reliable HTML sanitizer.

title: Reflected XSS: unescaped firstName echoed into an href attribute on the profile page
snippet: Google search this profile by name
evidence: `handleProfileUpdate` (POST /profile, guarded only by isLoggedIn) reads `firstName` from `req.body` (line 44) and, when the bankRouting regex check fails, assigns it unmodified to `firstNameSafeString` at app/routes/profile.js line 64 and renders it back via `res.render("profile", { ...,  firstNameSafeString, ... })`. app/views/profile.html renders that value unescaped inside an href attribute at line 78 (and inside a value attribute at line 41); server.js line 137 disables swig's autoescape application-wide, and CSRF protection is disabled (the `csrf()` middleware is commented out at server.js line 107), so the request that triggers this render can be forged cross-site.
impact: An attacker can submit `firstName` containing `"><script>...</script>` (or a `javascript:` URI) together with a bankRouting value chosen to fail validation, and because the value is echoed back unescaped into an href attribute, the injected markup/script executes in the victim's authenticated session; because CSRF protection is disabled, this can be triggered against a victim without their intentional participation.
fix: Re-enable swig's autoescape and HTML-encode firstName for the attribute context before rendering (or use a context-aware encoder such as node-esapi's encodeForHTMLAttribute), and re-enable CSRF protection on state-changing POST routes.

title: Reflected XSS: unescaped path parameter userId echoed into a form action attribute
evidence: GET /allocations/:userId (guarded only by isLoggedIn, app/routes/index.js line 63) destructures the raw route parameter into `userId` at app/routes/allocations.js line 18 and passes both the raw string (for rendering) and its `parseInt`-parsed form (for the DB lookup) onward; `parseInt` stops at the first non-digit character, so a value like `1"><script>alert(1)</script>` still resolves to user id 1 for the database query while the full raw string is rendered unescaped into the form's action attribute at app/views/allocations.html line 15 (server.js line 137 disables swig autoescape application-wide).
impact: An attacker can send a victim a link such as `/allocations/1%22%3E%3Cscript%3Ealert(document.cookie)%3C/script%3E` that resolves to a legitimate, existing user's allocations (via parseInt's lenient parsing) while injecting and executing arbitrary script in the victim's authenticated session.
fix: Re-enable swig's autoescape and validate that the userId route parameter is strictly numeric (reject the request instead of rendering it) before using it anywhere in the response.

title: Application only listens over plain HTTP, so credentials and the session cookie travel in cleartext
evidence: server.js starts the app with http.createServer(app).listen(...) at line 145, labelled by the developers' own comment on line 144 as the insecure path. The alternative https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...) block (lines 149-155) and the TLS key/cert loading it needs (lines 18-28) are both commented out, so no HTTPS listener is ever created; every request, including the POST /login body containing userName/password (app/routes/session.js handleLoginRequest) and the express-session cookie set on that response, is sent as plaintext.
impact: Anyone able to observe network traffic between the client and the server (a shared network, a compromised router, an on-path proxy) can read login credentials and the session cookie in the clear and hijack any user's session.
fix: Terminate TLS at the app or, at minimum, at a reverse proxy in front of it, and reinstate the commented-out https.createServer block (or run behind HTTPS termination with HSTS and secure cookies enforced end to end) rather than serving over http.createServer.

title: Session cookie is issued without HttpOnly, Secure or a non-default name, and never expires
evidence: The express-session options object passed to app.use(session({...})) has no cookie key at all: the block that would set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true } is commented out (lines 92-100), and the key: "sessionId" line that would rename the cookie away from the express-session default is also commented out (lines 87-90). With no cookie.httpOnly the cookie is readable from JavaScript by any script running on the page (including via XSS elsewhere in the app); with no cookie.secure it will also be sent over the plain-HTTP listener from the previous finding; with no cookie.maxAge/expires it persists until the browser session ends; and the cookie keeps express-session's default name connect.sid, which tells an attacker which session framework is in use.
impact: Any script injected into the page (stored/reflected XSS) or any network observer can read or replay a user's session cookie and take over their account; the cookie's default name also makes the app easier to fingerprint and target.
fix: Set cookie: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'strict', maxAge: <a bounded value> } and key: 'a-non-default-name' in the session() options, as the commented-out code already shows how to do.

title: CSRF protection (csurf) is installed but never mounted, and no CSRF token is issued to any form
evidence: The csurf package is a declared dependency (package.json line 11) and server.js even imports it at the top (line 7, also commented: `// const csrf = require('csurf');`), but the app.use(csrf()) call and the middleware that exposes res.locals.csrftoken to templates are both wrapped in a block comment and never executed. None of the state-changing POST routes registered in app/routes/index.js (/login, /signup, /profile, /contributions, /benefits, /memos) reference req.csrfToken() or a hidden CSRF field anywhere in their views, confirming no token is required to submit them. The session cookie also has no SameSite attribute (previous finding), so the browser will still attach it to a cross-site request.
impact: An attacker who gets a logged-in victim to load a crafted page can silently submit any of these POST endpoints on the victim's behalf — for example changing the victim's profile, contributions or benefits allocation — with no interaction beyond a page visit.
fix: Uncomment and mount app.use(csrf()) before the routes are registered, expose res.locals.csrftoken to the view layer, and add the hidden csrftoken field to every state-changing form.

title: Helmet is installed but never mounted: no CSP, no clickjacking protection, no HSTS, no MIME-sniffing protection, and X-Powered-By is left on
evidence: helmet is a declared dependency (package.json line 16) and is imported at server.js line 10 (also commented: `// const helmet = require("helmet");`), and dont-sniff-mimetype is imported at line 14 (also commented). The entire block that would call app.disable('x-powered-by'), helmet.frameguard(), helmet.noCache(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy(), helmet.hsts() and nosniff() is wrapped in a single /* ... */ block comment (lines 38-65) and none of it executes; I grepped the whole app/ tree for helmet, csurf and nosniff and the only other hits are the require lines above and the tutorial's own instructional HTML pages (app/views/tutorial/a5.html), not live route code. No response header is therefore set to restrict framing, restrict script/style sources, force HTTPS, or stop MIME-type sniffing, and the Express default X-Powered-By: Express header remains, disclosing the framework.
impact: The app can be framed by another site (clickjacking of the login/benefits/profile pages), has no Content-Security-Policy to contain any XSS that does occur, has no HSTS to prevent protocol downgrade once the HTTPS finding above is fixed, and lets a browser MIME-sniff responses; X-Powered-By also makes framework/version fingerprinting for an attacker trivial.
fix: Require and mount helmet() (or its individual middleware: frameguard, contentSecurityPolicy, hsts, noCache) and dont-sniff-mimetype before the routes are registered, and call app.disable('x-powered-by'), exactly as the commented-out code already does.

title: Swig template auto-escaping is disabled application-wide
evidence: consolidate.swig is registered as the view engine at server.js line 116, and swig.setDefaults is then called with autoescape: false; the developers' own commented-out replacement (autoescape: true, the swig default) is left in place labelled 'Fix for A3 - XSS', confirming this is a deliberately weakened default rather than an oversight. This setting applies to every .html view rendered through consolidate.swig, not to one route, so I mark it likely rather than confirmed: I read the global config but did not separately trace an attacker-controlled value into a specific {{ }} interpolation in a view for this finding (that is a separate per-sink review).
impact: Any view that interpolates request- or database-derived data (user names, profile fields, memo text, error messages) with the default {{ }} syntax will render it unescaped, turning what would otherwise be a safe-by-default template engine into one where every such interpolation is a potential stored or reflected XSS sink.
fix: Remove the autoescape: false override (or set it to true) so Swig's default HTML-escaping applies, and use the explicit unescape syntax only for the specific values that are verified safe to render as raw HTML.

title: The /learn route redirects to a URL taken directly from the query string
evidence: The handler for GET /learn takes req.query.url — fully attacker-controlled since it comes straight from the request URL — and passes it unvalidated into res.redirect(), with no allowlist of hosts or check that the value is a relative path. The developers' own comment on line 71 calls this out as insecure.
impact: An attacker can send a logged-in user a link such as /learn?url=https://evil.example/phish that the app will redirect to, which is useful for phishing (the link starts on the trusted nodegoat domain) or for chaining into open-redirect-based OAuth/SSO token theft if either is added later.
fix: Validate req.query.url against an allowlist of known-safe destinations or require it to be a relative path on the same origin before calling res.redirect(), or drop the query-string based redirect entirely in favor of a fixed set of named destinations.

title: The global error handler renders the raw Error object to the client
evidence: errorHandler (app/routes/error.js) is mounted last, after every route, via app.use(ErrorHandler) at app/routes/index.js line 82, so it does catch errors from any handler in the app (including MongoDB driver errors bubbled up with next(err) from the DAO callbacks). It logs err.message and err.stack to the server console (lines 7-8) but then also passes the whole err object as the error template variable at line 11, and app/views/error-template.html line 11 renders it directly as `{{error}}` with no field selection; since Swig auto-escaping is disabled app-wide (previous finding), that value is written into the HTML response unescaped.
impact: Any unhandled exception — including ones surfaced from library/database errors that were never meant for end users — is returned to the browser as the error object's string form, which can disclose internal implementation details (driver/library names, file paths in messages) useful for further attacks, and, because it is rendered unescaped, could itself be an XSS vector if any error message ever contains attacker-influenced text.
fix: In the error handler, log the full error server-side (as already done) but render a generic message plus a correlation id to the client instead of the err object itself, e.g. res.render('error-template', { error: 'An error occurred, reference: ' + correlationId }).

title: Admin account seeded with a hard-coded plaintext password used by the live login flow
evidence: artifacts/db-reset.js inserts USERS_TO_INSERT directly into the users collection via usersCol.insertMany (line 101); the admin record at line 14-20 carries the literal password "Admin_123" and isAdmin: true. This script is not a throwaway fixture: docker-compose.yml's web command runs `node artifacts/db-reset.js && npm start` before every container start, and app.json's Heroku "postdeploy" script is the same command, so this exact credential is what a docker-compose or Heroku deployment ends up with in its database. app/data/user-dao.js stores the password field verbatim (line 25, the bcrypt.hashSync alternative at line 29 is commented out) and validateLogin's comparePassword does `fromDB === fromUser` (line 61, the bcrypt.compareSync alternative at line 65 is commented out), so the seeded plaintext value is exactly what app/routes/session.js's handleLoginRequest checks against. The same file also seeds "user1"/"User1_123" (line 27) and "user2"/"User2_123" (line 35) with the identical pattern.
impact: Anyone who has read this public/committed file knows a working admin username and password for any deployment that used the stock seed script (the default docker-compose and Heroku one-click deploy paths both run it unmodified). Logging in as admin reaches the /benefits route gated by isAdminUserMiddleware and grants full access to every user's allocations, benefits and profile data in the application.
fix: Never ship a working credential in a seed script. Generate a random password per environment (or require an operator-supplied one via an environment variable) at seed time, hash it with bcrypt before insert (the code to do this already exists, commented out, in user-dao.js), and rotate the credential on any database that was ever seeded with the literal value above.

title: Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration
evidence: config/env/all.js exports this literal as part of the base config object. config/config.js (line 10) merges allConf with the per-NODE_ENV file using `{ ...allConf, ...envConf }`; none of development.js, test.js or production.js (all read) define a cookieSecret key, so this literal is the value in every environment, including production. server.js requires it directly (line 17: `const { port, db, cookieSecret } = require("./config/config")`) and passes it straight to express-session as the signing secret (line 82: `secret: cookieSecret`), with no environment-variable override anywhere in the codebase.
impact: Anyone with the repository (this is a public open-source project) has the exact secret express-session uses to sign the session-id cookie, letting them forge validly-signed session cookies and craft or tamper with session identifiers for any deployment that runs this config unmodified.
fix: Read the secret from an environment variable with no working default (`cookieSecret: process.env.COOKIE_SECRET` and fail startup if unset), generate a strong random value per deployment, and rotate the committed value.

owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
title: Full application config, including the session-cookie secret, is printed to the console on every startup
evidence: config.js builds `config` at line 10 from config/env/all.js, which includes the literal cookieSecret and cryptoKey values (all.js lines 8-9), then dumps the whole object with util.inspect at line 13. This module runs unconditionally on require, i.e. on every server start (server.js line 17 requires ./config/config), so the secrets are written to stdout/the process log on every boot, with no redaction.
impact: Anyone who can read the application's process logs (console output, a log aggregator, container logs, CI job output) obtains the session-signing secret and the configured crypto key without needing to read the source at all, widening who can reach secrets-002's impact beyond people with repository access.
fix: Remove the console.log of the full config object, or redact known-sensitive keys (cookieSecret, cryptoKey) before logging; if a startup config dump is needed for debugging, log only non-sensitive fields.

title: RSA private key committed to the repository in plaintext
snippet:
-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
[REDACTED PRIVATE KEY BODY]
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
evidence: This is a full, unencrypted PEM-encoded RSA private key committed at artifacts/cert/server.key. I traced its only reference in the codebase: server.js lines 18-28 contain a commented-out block that would do `fs.readFileSync(path.resolve(__dirname, "./artifacts/cert/server.key"))` and start an https.createServer with it (also commented out at lines 149-155); the server as actually run starts only `http.createServer` (line 145). So today this key is dormant — committed but not loaded by the running service, which serves plain HTTP. It would become live the moment an operator uncomments that block to "fix" the app's lack of TLS, which is exactly what the surrounding comments invite.
impact: Anyone with the repository holds the private half of the keypair matching artifacts/cert/server.crt. If this key is ever wired into a running HTTPS listener (as the commented-out code shows it is meant to be), anyone who has read this file can decrypt captured traffic to that listener or impersonate it in a machine-in-the-middle attack; today, with HTTPS disabled, the exposure is latent rather than actively reachable.
fix: Remove the private key from the repository, generate a fresh keypair with the CA/hosting provider used in production, and load it exclusively from a secrets manager or mounted volume outside version control; never commit private key material even for a demo TLS setup.

title: OWASP ZAP API key hard-coded in the default (development) environment config
evidence: development.js is config.js's default environment file: config.js line 5 picks `process.env.NODE_ENV || "development"`, so this literal is merged into the live config (`{ ...allConf, ...envConf }`, config.js line 10) whenever NODE_ENV is unset. The only consumer I found is test/security/profile-test.js (line 28: `var zapApiKey = config.zapApiKey;`), a Selenium+ZAP regression-test harness that uses it to authenticate to a local OWASP ZAP proxy instance for automated scanning — it is not read by server.js or any request-handling code. The identical literal is duplicated in config/env/test.js line 6.
impact: This key only controls a local ZAP proxy API (typically bound to 192.168.56.20:8080 per the same file, a private/test network), not the application's own authentication or data; its exposure lets someone who can already reach that ZAP instance control the security-scan session (e.g. wipe its session, run scans) rather than access application data or users.
fix: Even for a test-only tool credential, avoid a fixed literal shared across every checkout: generate it per test run or read it from an environment variable, since the value is otherwise permanently public in the repository history.

title: bcrypt-nodejs is unmaintained: last published in 2013, superseded by bcrypt/bcryptjs
evidence: package.json pins bcrypt-nodejs at the exact version 0.0.3. `npm view bcrypt-nodejs time --json` (registry query run in this review) shows 0.0.3, published 2013-02-25, is still the latest version on the registry: the package has had no release, security or otherwise, in over 12 years. It carries no open npm-audit advisory today, but a password-hashing library with no maintainer response is a standing risk (CWE-1104): any future flaw in its bcrypt implementation will never be patched upstream.
impact: No currently known CVE, so no immediate exploit; but the project's password hashing depends on a library nobody maintains, so any future vulnerability discovered in it (timing behavior, salt generation, native binding issues) has no upstream fix path and the application would carry it indefinitely.
fix: Migrate to the actively maintained `bcrypt` (native binding) or `bcryptjs` (pure JS) packages, which receive continued security maintenance.

title: body-parser range ^1.15.1 resolves to 1.18.3, vulnerable to two denial-of-service advisories
evidence: package.json declares body-parser ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves it to 1.18.3. `npm audit --json` run against the target's lockfile reports body-parser <1.20.3 as GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (high, CWE-405, denial of service when urlencoded parsing is enabled) and <1.20.6 as GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (low, CWE-770, invalid `limit` value silently disables size enforcement). Both ranges include the installed 1.18.3. body-parser is also a transitive dependency of the express install in this same tree, so the fix has to be applied consistently.
impact: A request crafted to exploit the urlencoded-body parsing path can exhaust CPU or memory on the request-handling process, denying service to legitimate users of the whole NodeGoat app (every route uses body-parser via express.js).
fix: Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 (or adopt express's now-bundled body parsing on express 4.16+/5.x) and re-run `npm audit`.

title: consolidate ^0.14.1 carries no current advisory but is templated around the also-abandoned swig engine
evidence: package-lock.json resolves consolidate to 0.14.5; it does not appear in the 145-package npm-audit result, so no known CVE is currently open against it. It is listed for completeness because it is the module that wires the app to the abandoned `swig` template engine (see the swig finding on line 22); its own risk is tied to what it loads.
impact: No standalone exploit path identified in this review.
fix: No action required against consolidate itself; address it together with the swig replacement (see the swig finding).

title: csurf is deprecated/archived upstream and pulls a vulnerable cookie parser
evidence: package.json declares csurf ^1.8.3, resolved to 1.9.0 in the lockfile. `npm view csurf deprecated` (registry query run in this review) returns: 'This package is archived and no longer maintained.' `npm audit --json` flags the installed range (>=1.3.0) as low severity because it depends on `cookie` <0.7.0, GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (CWE-74, cookie accepts name/path/domain values with out-of-bounds characters).
impact: Low on its own (the cookie issue needs an application that trusts unsanitized cookie attribute values), but csurf being archived means no future CSRF-related fix will ever ship for it, and its underlying double-submit-cookie design has known bypasses documented by its own maintainers in the deprecation notice.
fix: Replace csurf with a maintained CSRF middleware (e.g. `csrf-csrf` or a framework-level double-submit implementation) before its archived status becomes a liability.

title: dont-sniff-mimetype has no open advisory but has seen no release since 2015
evidence: Resolved to 1.0.0 in the lockfile; not present in the npm-audit vulnerability list. It sets the X-Content-Type-Options header, functionality now built directly into `helmet`, which this app also depends on, making the package redundant as well as stale.
impact: No known exploit; functional overlap with helmet increases the dependency surface for no benefit.
fix: Drop the dependency and rely on helmet's `noSniff()` middleware, which this app already installs.

title: express range ^4.13.4 resolves to 4.16.4, an old 4.x with open XSS/open-redirect advisories and 10 transitive advisory-carrying packages
evidence: package-lock.json resolves express to 4.16.4. `npm audit --json` reports the installed range (<=4.21.2) as high severity, naming GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (low, CWE-79, XSS via response.redirect() for versions <4.20.0) and GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (moderate, CWE-601/1286, open redirect on malformed URLs for versions <4.19.2); 4.16.4 falls in both vulnerable ranges. Walking the resolved dependency tree, express also pulls 10 other vulnerable packages (body-parser, cookie, debug, finalhandler, mime, ms, path-to-regexp, qs, send, serve-static), carrying 20 distinct advisories between them, several of which are independently listed as their own findings here (body-parser, cookie via csurf/express-session).
impact: An attacker who controls part of a redirect target reachable through app.js's routes can produce a reflected-XSS payload or redirect a victim to an attacker-controlled site under the app's own domain, undermining any anti-phishing assumption users make about links from the app.
fix: Upgrade express to at least 4.21.3, or move to the maintained 5.x line, then re-audit; this also picks up fixes in several of the ten transitively bundled packages.

title: express-session ^1.13.0 resolves to 1.15.6 and bundles a vulnerable cookie parser and on-headers
evidence: Resolved to 1.15.6. npm audit lists express-session's own advisory range (1.0.1-1.18.1) as low severity, inherited entirely from its two dependencies: `cookie` <0.7.0 (GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x, CWE-74) and `on-headers` <1.1.0 (GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q, CWE-241, HTTP response header manipulation). This is the middleware that issues NodeGoat's session cookie in app.js.
impact: The on-headers flaw lets a value already under attacker influence manipulate response headers set through it, which for a session middleware means a path toward header-injection-based cookie or cache-control tampering on the session cookie itself.
fix: Upgrade express-session to >=1.18.2 (pulls patched cookie and on-headers) and re-run npm audit to confirm the transitive advisories clear.

title: forever ^2.0.0 resolves to 2.0.0 (2015-era), a critical-severity direct dependency carrying 35 additional vulnerable transitive packages
evidence: package-lock.json resolves forever to 2.0.0. npm audit rates the installed range (>=0.7.4) critical and offers a fix only via a major upgrade to 4.0.3 (`npm view forever version` confirms 4.0.3 is the current published release, from 2022, so forever itself is still maintained upstream — this app is simply two majors behind). Walking forever's resolved subtree surfaces 35 further vulnerable packages beyond forever itself (nconf, flatiron, broadway, node-pre-gyp, tar, minimist, glob, semver, chokidar and others), 53 distinct GHSA advisories in total, several critical (e.g. GHSA-c2qf-rxjj-qqgw affecting bundled semver).
impact: forever is a process supervisor listed under production `dependencies` (not devDependencies), so its vulnerable tree ships into whatever environment runs `npm install --production`; the specific advisories in its tree include ReDoS and prototype-pollution issues that are reachable if forever's CLI or any of its bundled tooling processes attacker-influenced input (e.g. config parsing via nconf/ini).
fix: Upgrade to forever@4.0.3 (a breaking major-version change) or, if the goal is just process supervision in front of NodeGoat, replace it with a currently maintained process manager (e.g. pm2 or a systemd unit).

title: helmet ^2.0.0 resolves to 2.3.0, six majors behind current (8.x), with a moderate configuration-override advisory in its bundled helmet-csp
evidence: package-lock.json resolves helmet to 2.3.0; `npm view helmet version` shows the current release is 8.3.0. npm audit rates the installed range (0.3.0-3.20.1) high, driven by its dependencies `connect` and `helmet-csp`: GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c (moderate, Configuration Override in helmet-csp) plus debug's ReDoS advisories bundled via connect. Helmet is the security-headers middleware wired into app.js.
impact: The helmet-csp configuration-override flaw can let a later helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() call, or a merged config object, silently weaken the CSP the app believes it is enforcing, undermining the app's main defense-in-depth control against injected scripts.
fix: Upgrade to a current helmet major (8.x); the API changed significantly across majors 3-8, so this needs an app.js review of every `helmet.*()` call, not just a version bump.

title: marked is pinned to the exact version 0.3.5, vulnerable to ReDoS and two XSS-sanitization bypasses
evidence: package.json pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5 (no caret), matching what package-lock.json resolves. npm audit rates the installed range (<=4.0.9) high, listing six advisories that apply to 0.3.5 specifically: GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 (XSS via data URIs, <0.3.7), GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (HTML-entity sanitization bypass, <0.3.6), GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p (ReDoS, <0.3.9), GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, <0.3.17), plus two later ReDoS advisories affecting everything before 4.0.10. This is the markdown renderer app/routes/memos.js uses to render user-submitted memo text (per the app's own tutorial content).
impact: User-controlled markdown text rendered through marked 0.3.5 can carry a payload that bypasses its HTML-entity sanitization to achieve stored XSS, or a crafted input that triggers catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) and hangs the request-handling process.
fix: Upgrade marked to a current 4.x+ release (fixArray reports 0.3.19 as the minimal same-major fix, but the ReDoS advisories are only fully closed at >=4.0.10), and re-verify any output-escaping assumptions memos.js makes.

title: mongodb ^2.1.18 resolves to 2.2.36, a critical-severity driver bundling a bson deserialization flaw
evidence: package-lock.json resolves mongodb to 2.2.36. npm audit rates the installed range (<=3.1.12) critical: mongodb's own advisory GHSA-mh5c-679w-hh4r (high, denial of service, <3.1.13) applies, and its bundled `bson` <=1.1.3 carries GHSA-v8w9-2789-6hhr (critical, CWE-502, deserialization of untrusted data) plus GHSA-4jwp-vfvf-657p (moderate, same class); `mongodb-core` <=3.1.1 and `semver` are also flagged in the resolved subtree. This driver backs every DAO in app/data/*.js.
impact: bson deserializing untrusted data at critical severity means any code path that decodes attacker-influenced BSON/BSON-like structures (or a crafted query response) risks memory corruption or unexpected object construction inside the driver, on top of the driver's own DoS advisory; the mongodb 2.x line is also 5 majors behind the currently supported driver, so it will not receive further security backports.
fix: Upgrade the mongodb driver to a currently supported major (6.x or 7.x, matching your MongoDB server version), which is a breaking API change across every app/data/*.js file that uses it.

title: needle is pinned to the exact version 2.2.4 and carries a moderate-severity ReDoS in its bundled debug dependency
evidence: package.json pins needle to the exact version 2.2.4 (no caret), matched by the lockfile. needle itself has no direct advisory in the npm-audit output, but its dependency tree carries `debug` <4.3.1 (GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h, high, inefficient regex; GHSA-gxpj-cx7g-858c, low, ReDoS) and `ms`.
impact: Low on its own; the debug ReDoS advisories require the debug namespace to log attacker-controlled strings, which is plausible but not confirmed for needle's specific use in this codebase.
fix: Upgrade needle past 2.2.4 (a current 3.x release) to pick up a patched debug, or drop the exact pin so patch releases can flow through `npm audit fix`.

title: node-esapi is an unfinished, single-release ESAPI port with no release since 2014
evidence: package.json pins node-esapi to its only ever published version, 0.0.1. `npm view node-esapi time --json` (registry query run in this review) shows 0.0.1 published 2014-01-31 and still the latest: this is a 0.0.1 pre-release port of OWASP's ESAPI encoding/validation library that was never completed or maintained past its first publish. It is not in the npm-audit vulnerability list because no advisory has ever been filed against it, but a security-encoding library at version 0.0.1 with no subsequent release is not something to rely on for correctness.
impact: Any encoding/validation routine the app calls through node-esapi runs unaudited, unmaintained code; a gap or bug in its encoder (there is no changelog to confirm coverage) would ship silently into the app's output-encoding path with no upstream fix ever coming.
fix: Replace node-esapi with a maintained, actively-audited encoding library appropriate to the output context (e.g. the `he` package for HTML-entity encoding, or framework-level auto-escaping), and remove the ESAPI dependency once callers are migrated.

title: serve-favicon ^2.3.0 resolves to 2.5.0 and pulls a moderate-severity ReDoS via ms
evidence: Resolved to 2.5.0 in the lockfile. serve-favicon has no direct advisory in the npm-audit output; its dependency `ms` <2.0.0 carries GHSA-w9mr-4mfr-499f (moderate, ReDoS).
impact: Low: ms's ReDoS requires attacker-controlled input to reach ms's time-string parser, which serve-favicon does not expose directly.
fix: Upgrade serve-favicon to a release that pulls ms >=2.0.0, or run `npm audit fix`.

title: swig ^1.4.2 is deprecated upstream with an unfixed critical arbitrary-file-read advisory
evidence: package-lock.json resolves swig to 1.4.2, the last version swig's author ever published (`npm view swig time --json`, queried in this review, shows 1.4.2 published 2014-08-04 and still latest). `npm view swig deprecated` returns 'This package is no longer maintained.' npm audit rates the installed range (all versions, `*`) critical, naming GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (high, CWE-22, arbitrary local file read during template rendering) with `fixAvailable: false` — there is no patched version and there never will be. swig is one of the two template engines this app wires through `consolidate` (package.json line 10).
impact: If any swig template path is influenced by user input (a template name, a partial/include path derived from a request parameter), an attacker can read arbitrary files off the server filesystem through the template-rendering path; and because no fix exists, this risk cannot be closed by upgrading.
fix: Remove swig entirely and standardize on a maintained template engine already available in this stack (e.g. the other engine wired through consolidate), auditing every current .html template for swig-specific syntax that needs porting.

title: underscore ^1.8.3 resolves to 1.9.1, inside the range vulnerable to critical arbitrary code execution via template()
evidence: package-lock.json resolves underscore to 1.9.1. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.13.7) critical: GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (critical, CWE-94, arbitrary code execution in underscore's `template()` function for versions >=1.3.2 <1.12.1) directly applies to 1.9.1, and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (high, CWE-674/770, unbounded recursion in `_.flatten`/`_.isEqual`, <=1.13.7) also applies. `npm view underscore version` shows 1.13.8 is current and outside both vulnerable ranges.
impact: If any code path passes a template string influenced by user input into underscore's `_.template()` (directly, or indirectly through another library that wraps it), an attacker gets arbitrary JavaScript execution on the server; the recursion issue separately allows a denial of service via a deeply nested or self-referential input to `_.flatten`/`_.isEqual`.
fix: Upgrade underscore to >=1.13.8 and grep the codebase for any `_.template(` call sites to confirm none render request-controlled template strings.

title: async ^2.0.0-rc.4 resolves to 2.6.1, inside the range vulnerable to prototype pollution
evidence: package-lock.json resolves async to 2.6.1. npm audit rates the installed range (2.0.0-2.6.3) high, naming GHSA-fwr7-v2mv-hh25 (high, CWE-1321, prototype pollution, >=2.0.0 <2.6.4), which covers 2.6.1. `npm view async version` shows 3.2.6 is current, two majors ahead.
impact: async is a devDependency used by the build/test tooling (not shipped to the running app), so the practical exposure is limited to whoever runs `npm run test`/CI on untrusted input; within that scope, prototype pollution in async can corrupt shared object prototypes and change the behavior of unrelated code running in the same process.
fix: Upgrade async to >=3.2.6 (a breaking major change) or drop it if it's only pulled in transitively by other devDependencies.

title: cross-env ^7.0.2 pulls a high-severity command-injection-adjacent flaw in cross-spawn
evidence: Resolved to 7.0.2 exactly, no advisory against cross-env itself, but its dependency `cross-spawn` carries GHSA-3xgq-45jj-v275 (high, ReDoS in cross-spawn's command-line argument parsing).
impact: cross-env only runs during `npm run dev`/local scripts, so exposure is limited to a developer's own machine processing an unusual argument list; not attacker-reachable from the deployed app.
fix: Upgrade cross-env to a release that pulls a patched cross-spawn, or run `npm audit fix`.

title: cypress ^3.3.1 resolves to 3.3.1, a critical-severity release 13 majors behind current, carrying 29 further vulnerable packages
evidence: package-lock.json resolves cypress to 3.3.1. npm audit rates the installed range (0.1.0-15.15.0) critical with a fix only available at 16.1.0 (`npm view cypress version` confirms 16.1.0 is current). The resolved subtree carries 29 further vulnerable packages beyond cypress itself (request, tough-cookie, form-data, moment, lodash, qs, extract-zip, sshpk and others), 57 distinct advisories, several critical (e.g. lodash's GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 code injection via `_.template`, request's SSRF GHSA-jjv7-qpx3-h62q class of issues carried through its chain).
impact: cypress is a devDependency used for e2e testing (test/e2e/*), not shipped with the running app, so this does not directly expose production traffic; the risk is to whoever runs the e2e/CI pipeline against untrusted fixtures or in a shared CI environment where the bundled request/lodash/tough-cookie flaws could be triggered by a malicious test fixture or a compromised CI dependency.
fix: Upgrade cypress to the current major (16.x) as a dedicated migration, since the API and config format changed substantially since 3.x.

title: grunt ^1.0.3 resolves to 1.0.3, vulnerable to arbitrary code execution, a race condition and path traversal
evidence: package-lock.json resolves grunt to 1.0.3. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.6.1) critical, naming GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h (high, CWE-1188, arbitrary code execution, <1.3.0), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r (high, CWE-367, race condition, <1.5.3), and GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 (moderate, CWE-22, path traversal, <1.5.2) — all three ranges include 1.0.3. grunt drives this project's own build/test task runner (Gruntfile.js, `npm test`, `npm run db:seed`, `npm run precommit`). The resolved subtree also carries 16 further vulnerable packages (lodash, js-yaml, minimatch, glob, semver and others), 38 distinct advisories.
impact: grunt runs locally and in CI to build/test/seed the database; the arbitrary-code-execution and path-traversal advisories mean a malicious Gruntfile task definition or a crafted file processed by an outdated grunt task could execute code or read files outside the intended project directory during a build or CI run.
fix: Upgrade grunt to >=1.6.1 (npm audit reports a non-major fix is available) and re-run the full test/build pipeline.

title: grunt-cli ^1.2.0 resolves to 1.3.2, inside the moderate-severity range via its liftoff dependency
evidence: Resolved to 1.3.2. npm audit rates the installed range (1.3.0-1.3.2 || 1.4.1) moderate, inherited from `liftoff`; the resolved subtree separately carries 15 further vulnerable packages (debug, ini, micromatch, kind-of, set-value and the same brace-expansion/braces/fill-range chain seen under other grunt plugins), 13 distinct advisories.
impact: grunt-cli is the CLI entry point for the build/test pipeline; its own moderate-severity advisory chain is limited to local/CI execution, not the deployed app.
fix: Upgrade grunt-cli to >=1.5.0, which pulls a patched liftoff.

title: grunt-env is declared as the floating range "latest" and its currently-resolved version pulls a critical lodash advisory
evidence: package.json declares grunt-env as the literal string "latest" rather than a version or range — every `npm install` can resolve to whatever grunt-env's maintainers publish next, with no lockfile-enforced ceiling on what that pulls in. The lockfile currently resolves it to 1.0.1, which is not itself flagged, but its dependency `lodash` carries multiple advisories including GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695 (high, code injection via `_.template`) and GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw (critical, prototype pollution), 11 distinct advisories across ini and lodash in total.
impact: The floating "latest" declaration is itself a supply-chain exposure independent of today's resolved version (CWE-1357): a future grunt-env release could introduce new behavior or a new vulnerable dependency and it would install silently on the next `npm install` with no version bump to review in a diff.
fix: Pin grunt-env to an explicit version (matching what package-lock.json currently resolves, or newer), and upgrade the lodash it pulls in.

title: grunt-if is installed from a GitHub tarball pinned to the moving "master" branch, not a versioned registry release
evidence: package.json points grunt-if at `https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if/tarball/master` — a URL that resolves to whatever commit is HEAD on the `master` branch at install time, not a fixed, reviewable release (CWE-829, inclusion of functionality from an untrusted/unpinned control sphere). Separately, `npm view grunt-if version` shows the package's own last registry release was 0.1.5, published 2015-02-26 — over a decade with no update — and npm audit rates the resolved dependency (via grunt-contrib-jshint's own advisory chain) high severity; walking its resolved subtree surfaces 66 further vulnerable packages and 98 distinct advisories, several critical (grunt's own code-execution/path-traversal advisories, babel/istanbul chains, request's SSRF class issues).
impact: Because the dependency is fetched from a mutable branch reference rather than a pinned tag/commit or a registry version, the exact code that lands in node_modules on any given `npm install` is not reproducible and not something the lockfile's integrity hash actually protects the way it does for registry packages: a compromise of that GitHub repository's master branch, or a maintainer force-push, changes what code every future install runs with no corresponding change to review in this project's own history.
fix: Replace grunt-if with a maintained, registry-published alternative, or at minimum pin the tarball URL to an exact commit SHA and vendor/verify that commit's contents; either way, this is a decade-unmaintained micro-package that should be removed from the build.

title: grunt-contrib-jshint ^3.0.0 resolves to 3.2.0 and pulls a high-severity ReDoS via its own bundled jshint
evidence: Resolved to 3.2.0. npm audit rates the installed range (`*`, i.e. all published versions) high, inherited from its dependency `jshint`, itself vulnerable via `minimatch` (GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, high, CWE-400, ReDoS) and `shelljs` (GHSA-6c8f-qphg-qjgp/GHSA-952p-6rrq-rcjv, CWE-269, improper privilege management). npm audit reports no fix is available (`fixAvailable: false`) for grunt-contrib-jshint at its current major line.
impact: Runs during local linting/CI only; a crafted source file processed by the vulnerable minimatch pattern matching could hang the lint task via catastrophic backtracking.
fix: There is no in-range fix; either accept the risk for a CI-only tool with no attacker-reachable input, or replace grunt-contrib-jshint with a maintained ESLint-based grunt task.

title: grunt-contrib-watch >=0.5.0 is flagged high severity and its resolved subtree carries 12 further vulnerable packages
evidence: Resolved to 1.1.0. npm audit rates the installed range (>=0.5.0) high, with a fix only available via a major downgrade to 0.4.4 per its metadata — in practice this means using the current 1.1.0 release and upgrading its own dependency chain instead. The resolved subtree carries 12 further vulnerable packages (gaze, globule, websocket-driver, websocket-extensions, qs, debug, lodash and the same glob/minimatch/brace-expansion chain seen elsewhere), 34 distinct advisories.
impact: grunt-contrib-watch runs a local filesystem watcher during development; its websocket-driver/websocket-extensions advisories matter if the dev server's live-reload channel is ever exposed beyond localhost.
fix: Upgrade the dependencies grunt-contrib-watch pulls in (gaze, globule, websocket-driver) to their patched releases and re-audit; consider replacing it with `nodemon` (already a devDependency) for file-watching.

title: grunt-npm-install bundles an old npm CLI with permission and arbitrary-file-write advisories
evidence: Resolved to 0.3.1. npm audit rates its resolved range (`*`) moderate, entirely inherited from the bundled `npm` package it shells out through, which carries GHSA-c6rq-rjc2-86v2 (high, CWE-732, incorrect permission assignment for a critical resource), GHSA-hmw2-7cc7-3qxx (arbitrary file write, CWE-59/61), and GHSA-qrmc-fj45-qfc2 (symlink escape outside node_modules, CWE-22). npm audit reports no fix is available for grunt-npm-install itself (`fixAvailable: false`). Its resolved subtree carries 34 further vulnerable packages, 70 distinct advisories.
impact: This grunt task shells out to run `npm install` as part of the build; the bundled npm's file-write/permission advisories could let a malicious package.json or a compromised transitive package escalate its install-time footprint (e.g. write outside node_modules) during that step.
fix: Drop grunt-npm-install and run `npm install` directly as a build step (invoking the system's own current npm) instead of depending on a bundled, unpatched copy.

title: grunt-retire — the task meant to catch outdated dependencies — is itself years out of date and pulls a critical advisory through its own `underscore` dependency
evidence: Resolved to 0.3.12; `npm view grunt-retire version` shows 1.0.9 is current, and its own `retire` dependency in turn depends on `underscore`, which is independently flagged critical in this report (dep-underscore, GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq, arbitrary code execution) and on `request`, flagged for SSRF-class advisories (GHSA-jp4x-w63m-7wgm and related). npm audit rates grunt-retire's own resolved range (>=0.1.1) moderate.
impact: The irony is functional as well as reputational: this project's own dependency-vulnerability scanner is running an outdated copy that shares the underscore/request risk it exists to catch, and cannot be trusted to have current advisory data at 0.3.12 either.
fix: Upgrade grunt-retire to 1.0.9, or replace it with `npm audit`/`osv-scanner` run directly in CI, which is what this review used.

title: jshint is pinned to the exact version 2.12.0 and carries a high-severity ReDoS via its bundled minimatch
evidence: package.json pins jshint to the exact version 2.12.0 (no caret). npm audit rates the installed range (0.5.0 || >=0.6.0, i.e. effectively all releases) high, inherited from `minimatch` (GHSA-hxm2-r34f-qmc5, CWE-400, ReDoS) and `shelljs` (CWE-269, improper privilege management). `npm view jshint version` shows 2.13.6 is current. No fix is available in-range (`fixAvailable: false`).
impact: jshint lints source files during CI/local development only; the ReDoS is reachable if a crafted source file's glob pattern matching hangs the lint step, a low-severity nuisance for a CI-only tool with no attacker-facing input in this app.
fix: Upgrade jshint to 2.13.6, and remove the exact-version pin so future patch releases can flow through `npm audit fix`.

title: mocha ^2.4.5 resolves to 2.5.3, inside the critical range because its bundled growl allows command injection
evidence: Resolved to 2.5.3. npm audit rates the installed range (0.6.0-6.2.2) critical, driven by `growl` <1.10.0, GHSA-qh2h-chj9-jffq (critical, CWE-78/94, command injection in growl's desktop-notification shell-out). `npm view mocha version` shows 12.0.2 is current, ten majors ahead.
impact: mocha runs the test suite locally/in CI; growl's command injection triggers when mocha's desktop-notification reporter is used with attacker-influenced test names or output, which is plausible in a CI environment that runs against untrusted branches/PRs.
fix: Upgrade mocha to a current major (12.x); this drops the vulnerable growl dependency entirely (later mocha versions do not ship it).

title: nodemon ^1.19.1 resolves to 1.19.1, a high-severity release with 36 further vulnerable packages in its resolved subtree
evidence: package-lock.json resolves nodemon to 1.19.1, matching the exact floor of the declared range. npm audit rates the installed range (1.3.5-2.0.16, || 2.0.18) high, with a fix only via the major upgrade to 3.1.14 (`npm view nodemon version` confirms 3.1.14 is current). Its resolved subtree carries 36 further vulnerable packages (chokidar, got, update-notifier, boxen, term-size, package-json and the fill-range/braces/micromatch chain), 53 distinct advisories.
impact: nodemon only runs the local dev server (`npm run dev`); its update-notifier/package-json chain makes outbound registry requests that a compromised transitive dependency could abuse, but it never runs in the deployed environment described by the Dockerfile/Procfile.
fix: Upgrade nodemon to 3.1.14 for local development use.

title: selenium-webdriver ^2.53.2 resolves to 2.53.3, pulling adm-zip's uncontrolled-memory-allocation and ws's memory-exhaustion advisories
evidence: Resolved to 2.53.3. npm audit rates the installed range (2.43.1-4.0.0-rc-2) high, inherited from `adm-zip` <=0.6.0 (GHSA-xcpc-8h2w-3j85, high, CWE-400/789, crafted ZIP triggers 4GB allocation; GHSA-7q85-xj36-vmfc, high, uncontrolled memory allocation via declared size) and `xml2js` (GHSA-776f-qx25-q3cc, moderate, prototype pollution). `npm view selenium-webdriver version` shows 4.49.0 is current.
impact: selenium-webdriver drives local/e2e browser automation only; the adm-zip advisories matter if it ever unpacks a driver binary or extension archive from an untrusted source during test setup.
fix: Upgrade selenium-webdriver to 4.49.0 (a breaking major change) as part of the same e2e-tooling refresh as cypress.

title: zaproxy <=1.0.1 pulls lodash's critical code-injection advisory and request's SSRF-class advisories
evidence: Resolved to 0.2.0. npm audit rates the installed range (<=1.0.1) moderate at the package's own level, but its dependencies `lodash` (GHSA-jf85-cpcp-j695, high, code injection via `_.template`; GHSA-p6mc-m468-83gw, critical, prototype pollution) and `request` (GHSA-jp4x-w63m-7wgm and related, moderate SSRF-class issues) push the effective severity of running this tool to critical. `npm view zaproxy version` shows 2.0.0-rc.7 is current.
impact: zaproxy is a Node.js client for the OWASP ZAP security scanner, used here as devDependency tooling; its lodash chain's code-injection risk applies if the tool ever templates a value derived from scan results or configuration that an attacker influences (e.g. a scan target's response content reflected back into a report template).
fix: Upgrade zaproxy to 2.0.0-rc.7 or later, which pulls patched lodash/request.
